chunks: From him, from Safwan and Fadalah, from al-Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), and Hammad from Hariz, from Muhammad, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him).

Regarding a man who had dirhams owed to him by another man, so he sold him pigs and wine while watching him, and then he paid him off. He said: 'There is no objection to it; as for the one who received the payment (the creditor), it is permissible, and as for the seller (the debtor), it is forbidden.'

key_terms.البَائِعِ: the seller (the debtor who sells the item to pay)
key_terms.المَقْضِيِّ: the creditor (one who receives the payment)

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible to pay off a debt with pigs or wine?
ai.summary: Recorded in Shaykh al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, this hadith from Imam al-Baqir (AS) clarifies the dual nature of debt settlement using impure goods (najis), distinguishing between the creditor’s right to accept them as valid discharge (halal for the recipient) and the debtor’s act of using them as payment (haram for the payer). This ruling highlights the Shia jurisprudential principle that the impurity of the item does not invalidate the contractual obligation, yet the specific context of 'looking at' the transaction underscores the voluntary acceptance by the creditor. It serves as a key precedent in the chapter of *Gharar* (uncertainty) and *Mujafafa* (speculation), illustrating how physical purity is separate from legal validity in debt resolution.
